item.title: What to Know About Today’s U.K. Special Election: Farage vs. Binface
item.description:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform U.K., Britain’s populist right-wing party, will face voters on Thursday in a special election that he initiated, hoping to return to Parliament weeks after resigning amid investigations into possible financial impropriety.

Mr. Farage, who is under investigation for failing to declare a 5 million pound gift (about $6.7 million) from a British crypto-billionaire in Thailand, has said he hopes that a new mandate from his constituents in Clacton, a coastal area in Essex, England, will show that his voters do not care about the issue.

He said that he has been the subject of “constant demonization” by the press and his critics. The investigations into his finances, he claims, are proof that the “establishment have now decided that they can’t beat us fairly, so they’ve chosen to use foul means.”

After he resigned to force the new special election, all of Britain’s major parties boycotted it, calling it a stunt. Mr. Farage’s most significant opponent is a novelty candidate named Count Binface, who campaigns wearing a trash can over his head.

Here’s what to know about Thursday’s vote.

As the leader of Reform U.K., Mr. Farage is the most prominent right-wing populist in Britain, focused on campaigning against immigration and in favor of lower taxes and fewer regulations, particularly on cryptocurrency.

A veteran politician who campaigned for more than two decades for Britain to leave the European Union, and who has led several parties, Mr. Farage is an ally of President Trump and has styled himself in a similar way. He has long warned of an “invasion” of migrants and railed against the establishment in Westminster.

For most of the last year, Reform led national opinion polls amid widespread concern about rising prices, taxes, migration and dissatisfaction with Keir Starmer, the former Labour prime minister.

In May, Mr. Farage led Reform to its biggest electoral success ever. The party won almost 1,500 seats on municipal councils. But overall, Reform won only about 26 percent of the vote, down from more than 30 percent the previous year.

And the party has lost several parliamentary by-elections that it had hoped to win in recent months, including in Gorton and Denton, which was won by the Green Party, and in Makerfield, where Labour’s Andy Burnham easily beat the Reform candidate.

The polls have shown a continued decline for Reform in recent weeks, as the accusations about improper disclosure of financial support have increased. Several recent polls have shown support for the party falling under 25 percent and Labour taking the lead.

Earlier this year, Britain’s parliamentary standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, confirmed that he was investigating whether Mr. Farage had broken parliamentary rules by not disclosing the £5 million gift from Christopher Harborne, the crypto billionaire.

Mr. Farage has said he did not need to disclose the gift, but has offered a variety of conflicting explanations for why Mr. Harborne gave him the money in the weeks before he won his seat in Parliament in 2024.

He initially said it was for his personal security amid threats. In his resignation speech, he said that he gets “daily online calls for me to be murdered” and has run up “very, very substantial bills to make sure that I was safe.”

But in an interview in May, Mr. Farage said the money was “a reward for campaigning for Brexit.”

Critics of Mr. Farage have pointed out that since he entered Parliament, he has championed the cryptocurrency industry and that Reform has pushed for light-touch regulation.

In his resignation speech, Mr. Farage referred to the standards investigation into the Harborne gift, but also said that “yet another standards investigation is underway.” That comment came days after The Sunday Times of London reported that one of his close aides, George Cottrell, had provided undisclosed benefits to Mr. Farage including security, social media employees and accommodation.

Mr. Farage did not intend to stay out of office for long.

In his remarks last month announcing his resignation, he said that “the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions. This will be a people-versus-the-establishment by-election. It’s a chance to stick two fingers up to the entire establishment, to frankly tell them where to go.”

Reform officials were always very confident that Mr. Farage would recapture his seat in Parliament. The last time he ran in Clacton, during the 2024 general election, he won with 46.2 percent of the vote. The Conservative Party candidate came second with 27.9 percent.

But Mr. Farage and his advisers hoped to use the election to change the political narrative and give him a prominent victory over his major rival political parties. Instead, all of the main parties said they would not put forward candidates, preferring to wait for the results of the parliamentary investigation.

That makes it more likely that Mr. Farage will win a landslide, while making it harder for him to argue that he defeated “the establishment.”

Count Binface is a character played by Jon Harvey, 46, a writer and comedian who is part of Britain’s long tradition of novelty political candidates. He describes himself as an intergalactic space warrior from the planet Sigma IX. His campaign pledges include a promise to build “at least one affordable house” and to “cut your taxes and raise everyone else’s.”

Mr. Harvey — or, as he’s better known, Mr. Binface — has run in several recent elections. In the recent special election where Prime Minister Andy Burnham won with 24,927 votes, Mr. Binface received just 95. (Though that was more than twice the number of votes that Howling Laud Hope received as the candidate for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party.)

In a recent interview in The New York Times, Mr. Binface said, “If humans choose to vote for Nigel, that is democracy.” But with the major parties absent, “I seem to be his majesty’s opposition.”

He is not expected to win on Thursday.

Assuming that Mr. Farage wins, as expected, he will once again be a member of Parliament. But the investigations into his finances — and those of Reform U.K. — are unlikely to be resolved any time soon.

The parliamentary standards investigation could continue for weeks or months.

If the standards investigation concludes that Mr. Farage violated Parliament’s rules, he could be suspended, possibly prompting another special election. The Conservative Party has already said it would run a candidate in Clacton if that happens.

There is also a police investigation underway into the legality of two donations to Reform of £250,000 each from Mr. Cottrell’s mother, Fiona. In a statement last month, the Metropolitan Police said that two people had been questioned as part of the investigation, although no arrests have been made. Reform did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. Cottrell and Ms. Cottrell could not be reached for comment.

item.title: Israel Evicted Settlers Besieging Palestinian Homes. Hours Later, They Were Back.
item.description:
The Israeli military evicted on Thursday about a dozen settlers who had besieged two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes, but several hours later settlers returned.

The Palestinian families had been trapped in their homes since Sunday by Israeli settlers, who had erected a tent nearby and, residents said, attacked them, including with rocks.

On Thursday morning, Israeli soldiers dismantled structures set up in the area by the settlers, confiscated some equipment, detained one settler and dispersed the rest, according to a military statement.

The operation came after heightened media attention, including the disclosure that one of the homes’ owners, Louai Abu Ridi, 46, is an American citizen. Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, condemned the settlers and said the United States had urged Israel to intervene.

“The actions of those doing this to this family’s home is criminal,” wrote Mr. Huckabee, a longtime supporter of the settler movement. He said, “Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting.”

But just hours after the eviction operation ended in the village of Qusra, located in the northern West Bank, at least nine settlers returned to the site where they were previously encamped outside one of the homes, according to interviews with two residents and video footage reviewed by The New York Times.

“We are still under siege,” said Yousef Hassan, 30, who remains locked inside with his brother and his son. “If the army is here to take out the settlers, why are they not just doing it?” he asked.

Mr. Hassan said his family was running low on food and water.

The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The military on Thursday also evicted settlers who had taken over another Palestinian house in nearby Jalud, according to its residents. Here, too, the settlers returned shortly after.

The military’s failure to keep settlers away from Qusra village after waiting several days before evicting them underscored the challenge it faces in contending with settler violence. It also highlights the deepening chaos across the West Bank, where hundreds of Israeli settlers have terrorized Palestinian communities with near-impunity all year.

Extremist settlers have carried out at least 1,380 attacks across 250 communities in 2026, according to U.N. data from late July. Those settlers have faced a near-total lack of consequences for their violence.

Former senior Israeli officials who previously oversaw the West Bank now warn that the military is losing its grip on the territory and allowing settlers to run wild.

“The Israeli military lost control in the West Bank,” said Guy Hazut, a reserve brigadier general who once oversaw parts of the territory as a commander.

The settlers seek to drive Palestinians from their land and have displaced several entire communities over the past three years.

The families in Qusra have refused to leave their homes even in the face of persistent attacks.

“We are very afraid,” said Aisha Hassan, 35, who said she was still besieged in her home with her elderly mother on Thursday. “But we won’t leave. Even if it’ll get us killed.”

Adam Rasgon and Gabby Sobelman contributed reporting.

item.title: As Europe Gets Hotter, Its Transportation Systems Struggle to Cope
item.description:
Tracks are buckling in Sweden. Highways are cracking in Germany. Commuters are sweltering in airless train carriages across the world’s fastest-warming continent.

This is the new reality in Europe, where much of the transportation infrastructure was not built to withstand the scorching summer heat that’s becoming routine.

“Europe’s transport systems were engineered for a climate that no longer exists,” Patrice Geoffron, who leads the energy and climate economics team at Université Paris Dauphine-PSL in France, wrote in an email.

Many of Europe’s tracks and roads desperately need upgrades to meet new extreme temperature thresholds, or delays and disruptions will become the norm, experts said. Rail services in Britain and France reduced services this week and warned of disruptions as Western Europe endured its fifth heat wave since May,

The changes needed to fully accommodate the effects of global warming would require vast amounts of money. And even if cash-strapped European governments had those funds, many countries are focused more on defense than on infrastructure, experts said. For now, they are mostly making smaller adjustments.

“The main challenge is actually not heat; the main challenge is funding itself,” said Prof. Felix Creutzig of the University of Sussex, who leads the working group on cities at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research near Berlin.

Disruptions from the heat are most obvious on Europe’s trains, which hundreds of millions of people use in cities and to cross the countryside. Many of these rail systems are generations old, said Ian Mulcahey, the global director of cities at Gensler, an international architecture and planning firm. (London’s metro, the world’s oldest, opened in 1863.)

Many of these systems still rely, to some degree, on dated infrastructure. Many European train carriages don’t have air-conditioning.

Some systems are incorporating new technologies as they expand and update. Mr. Mulcahey pointed to the air-conditioned Elizabeth Line in London, a major east-west artery that opened in 2022 and cost about 19 billion pounds ($25.5 billion). Others are making smaller changes. France’s state-owned railway operator, for instance, says it is adapting stations for extreme weather.

But it’s not possible to start from scratch.

“The challenge for us in Europe is, how do you go back and retrospectively adapt your infrastructure for a new age?,” said Mr. Mulcahey, who specializes in large-scale city planning.

On Thursday, a train derailed near Lewes, in southern England, injuring two, as Britain recorded its hottest day of the summer so far. It was not immediately clear whether the accident was heat related.

“But we do know that the rail companies have been reporting that the extreme dry conditions have been affecting embankments and track conditions,” James MacCleary, a lawmaker representing Lewes, told Times Radio on Thursday. “We had a lot of speed restrictions in the area recently, which is directly related to the heat.”

For trains, extreme heat poses three main problems:

Most aren’t air-conditioned. Europe is not known for air-conditioning — until recently, summers seldom got hot enough to need it with any regularity — and generally speaking, the continent’s trains are no exception.

That is changing, often as part of broader upgrades, but it is a slow and expensive process. London is spending an estimated £3.4 billion ($4.6 billion) to replace the carriages on another metro line, the Piccadilly, with a streamlined new fleet whose features include air-conditioning. And that is just one of the 11 lines in the city’s underground system, known as the Tube.

Mr. Mulcahey said Londoners were starting to modify their commutes to spend at least part of them on air-conditioned routes, like the Elizabeth Line or the city’s overground trains.

Discomfort aside, overheated trains can lead to heat exhaustion and worse. Many carriage windows don’t open, and if a train should lose power, the situation could become dangerous under a scorching sun. Although heat — like fire — can be deadly, it probably wouldn’t occur to passengers to use emergency hammers to break the windows, said Jennifer Schooling, a professor at Anglia Ruskin University and a director of DARe, a research center in Britain that studies the effects of global warming on transportation.

Heat can warp the tracks. Tracks are made of metal, which expands in the heat. Many of Europe’s were built decades ago, designed for less extreme temperatures, and lately they have been buckling and twisting.

A “sun curve” — that is, a rail bending sideways in extreme heat — is believed to have caused a freight train derailment in Sweden in June, the Swedish Transport Administration said.

Experts say a cheap adaptation to this problem is available by painting the tracks white, which creates a cooling effect by reflecting back sunlight. (Britain does this for “hot spots” on its rails.)

But that stopgap fix is no substitute for an expensive, wholesale replacement of track, said Prof. François Gemenne, the academic director of the master’s program in sustainability and social innovation at HEC Paris, a business school.

“You can win a couple of years with that,” Professor Gemenne said of lighter coloring. “But at some point, you will need to have rails that can withstand much higher temperatures.”

Power lines are vulnerable, too. The overhead wires that supply power to electric trains can expand in extreme heat, just as tracks do. Sometimes, older or badly maintained lines droop so low that they get caught on a moving train.

That can cause a power outage and, occasionally, a cascading series of problems along the rail network. “One incident can block a busy corridor, trap rolling stock and crews in the wrong locations and generate delays and cancellations,” Professor Geoffron said. One such incident in the Netherlands last month disrupted traffic between Britain, France, Belgium and Germany, he said.

Some newer cables have automated systems that adapt to temperature fluctuations, using balance weights or springs to loosen or tighten as needed. But the tension in older cables is fixed, and if they’re too tight, they can snap in the wintertime, Professor Schooling said.

“We’re in this conundrum,” she said. “The impacts of climate change seem to be happening faster than we were expecting.”

Many of Europe’s roads weren’t built for today’s extreme temperatures, either. Roads made with concrete can crack if they don’t have room to expand in the heat. Such “blowups” forced the partial closure of German highways this summer.

Road surfaces can melt, too, a phenomenon that has caused disruptions from Britain to Sweden. During Europe’s June heat wave, trams were halted in the German city of Leipzig because asphalt had melted and gummed up the tracks.

As with railroad tracks, lighter colors can keep road surfaces cooler, Professor Geoffron said. Roads can also be made with materials that are more heat resistant than traditional asphalt. But those materials are often more expensive and require more exacting construction, he said.

During recent heat waves, trucks that spread salt during winter storms laid down sand or dust on some English streets to keep melting road surfaces from getting too sticky.

Even that low-budget fix can be tricky, Professor Schooling said. Too much sand, and cars could start to skid.

item.title: Five Arrested in Connection to Stolen Works by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse, Prosecutors Say
item.description:
It took thieves less than three minutes, the police said, to make off with three artworks by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse worth millions of dollars during a bold nighttime heist in March.

On Friday, Italian officials announced that they had arrested five people in connection to the theft and recovered the art.

The Carabinieri, Italy’s military police, said in a statement that the recovery had followed “a complex investigation” overseen by the Parma public prosecutor’s office.

Following up on clues left at the scene of the crime and wiretaps, the authorities tracked down “a group of professional thieves,” Col. Andrea Pagliaro, the commander of the carabinieri unit that led the investigation, said in a telephone interview. The suspects are all from Moldova, he said.

On Friday morning, police found the three artworks in the storage room of a home in Parma, hidden inside an empty television cardboard box, he said.

The police released a video of the March heist captured by cameras inside its target, the Magnani-Rocca Foundation, a private art museum outside Parma, northern Italy. The video highlighted the ease with which the artworks were taken.

The artworks are:

Paul Cézanne’s “Still Life With Cherries,” a pencil and watercolor work valued at 6 million euros, or roughly $7 million.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s “Les Poissons,” an oil painting valued at €3 million, roughly $3.5 million.

Henri Matisse’s “Odalisque Sur La Terrasse,” an etching valued at €20,000, roughly $23,000.

The video showed two masked figures slipping into the museum in the early hours of March 23 after breaking the glass panel of the front door, flashlights fixed to their heads. It then showed them moving through the museum atrium, entering the room where the three works hung and easily lifting them from the walls.

Then the video cut back to the front hall, where one intruder passed two artworks through the front door to a waiting accomplice, before the second approached the door, carrying the third work.

Colonel Pagliaro said the video showed that the thieves had been “very organized,” working quickly and managing to deactivate the alarms with electronic devices.

The suspects had been based in Parma and some had lived there “for many years,” he said.

“Finding the works was the most important thing,” Colonel Pagliaro said, in particular because the suspects had begun to look for buyers, “even through international channels.”

Four of the five people arrested participated in the theft at the museum, while the artworks were found in the home of the fifth, said Lieut. Col. Giuseppe Marseglia, who oversaw the investigation on the part of Italy’s art-theft squad.

He said the group was not specialized in art thefts. “This was our advantage,” he said. “They thought it would be easy,” but they didn’t know how to sell works on the art market.

He said the group had been identified not long after the theft, but it took time to track down the possible places where the works could have been hidden.

The raid made headlines worldwide, coming some five months after burglars broke into the Apollo Gallery at the Louvre in Paris in daylight, making off with eight pieces of crown jewelry valued at more than $100 million.

The Magnani-Rocca Foundation was founded in the 1970s by Luigi Magnani, an Italian intellectual and collector. The collection includes work from several countries and centuries, including paintings by Goya, Titian, Dürer, and Van Dyck, as well as works by the 20th-century Italian artist Giorgio Morandi.

Stefano Roffi, who oversees the collection. said the theft had left colleagues “devastated,” and that the three works’ return called for “a fitting celebration,” according to an interview with ANSA, the main Italian news agency.

Lieutenant Colonel Marseglia said that immediately after the theft, the paintings had been listed on various sites that track stolen artworks, including Interpol. “That made them effectively unsaleable,” he said.

item.title: Zambia Halts Vote Counting in Presidential Race
item.description:
Zambian officials suspended vote counting in the presidential race on Friday, citing violence against poll workers and the theft of ballots in the southern African nation.

The move raised fears among opposition leaders that the results could be tampered with in the contest. Both candidates had claimed an advantage in early tallies.

President Hakainde Hichilema has been favored to win a second term, but economic hardship and concerns over growing repression have tightened the race.

Mr. Hichilema’s main opponent, Brian Mundubile, claimed victory in a statement on Friday, citing an unofficial vote count led by his party and early polling results. He said the suspension of vote counting by the Electoral Commission of Zambia raised “legitimate fears that this delay could create an opportunity for interference with, or manipulation of the results.”

Mulambo Haimbe, an official in Mr. Hichilema’s party, the United Party for National Development, said the concerns of election rigging were “purely speculative,” and accused Mr. Mundubile of “inciting the people to an uprising.”

He also said that early indications after Thursday’s vote were positive for Mr. Hichilema, adding that turnout had been high in his strongholds.

The party also saw positive results for Mr. Hichilema in places where the president underperformed in the last election, Mr. Haimbe said.

Both candidates have called for a speedy resumption of the vote count, and the electoral commission said it would review the suspension within 24 hours. Results were initially scheduled to be finalized by Monday. It is unclear how the suspension will affect that timeline.

To win the presidential election in Zambia, a candidate must get more than 50 percent of the vote. If that does not happen in the first round of voting, the top two candidates compete in a runoff.

When Mr. Hichilema rose to power five years ago, he was seen as a bright spot for democracy in Africa. He had unsuccessfully vied for the office several times before and had been subjected to what analysts saw as a political imprisonment by the government he challenged.

The incumbent at the time, Edgar Lungu, was accused of suppressing the opposition and influencing the vote. Having overcome those challenges, Mr. Hichilema promised to renew Zambia’s democracy.

But during his five years in power, his government has passed measures that human rights groups say restrict press freedom and muzzle critics of his administration. In the lead up to this year’s election, Mr. Hichilema and his party were accused of violently cracking down on opposition rallies and thwarting political opponents from entering the race.

Mr. Hichilema, who has denied allegations of repression, had based his campaign on his success reviving Zambia’s stagnant economy. He helped the country climb out of crushing debt. He has attracted investors back to the country and pumped life into the vital mining sector, with Zambia being one of the world’s top copper producers.

But those high-level economic victories have not translated to a better life for many in Zambia, where many still face rising food and fuel prices and high unemployment.

Rabecca Lungu contributed reporting from Lusaka, Zambia.

item.title: When a Rare Wolf Got Too Close, Denmark Faced a Conservation Dilemma
item.description:
On Friday morning, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare stood before reporters to declare that a serious threat had been eliminated. On the lawn a few feet away, beneath a white sheet, lay the body of a young male wolf.

For more than a week, the authorities had hunted it down like a fugitive: armed officers marched through the woods, thermal drones zipped in the skies and residents called in sightings.

“It has been an intensive effort,” said Christian Rabjerg Madsen, the minister.

Then he stood back as a wildlife officer slowly pulled away the white sheet, revealing the dead wolf, killed by a fatal shot to its right flank.

Denmark has an estimated 49 wolves, part of a growing European population. Their return has been hailed as a conservation success. But in countries such as France, Spain, Italy, Sweden and now Denmark, the wolves have brought growing conflicts over livestock, public safety and how to manage the species.

Wolves were believed to have disappeared from Denmark in the early 1800s, because of over-hunting. But they reappeared in 2012 after migrating through Germany. Since then, the animals have become a recurring source of controversy, attacking livestock and, in some instances, getting killed illegally, possibly by angry farmers. This takedown, however, is the first time in years officers killed a wolf themselves.

This young wolf, lean with light brown fur, raised concerns earlier this month after a string of encounters around Norre Nebel, a small town 170 miles west of Copenhagen. Witnesses reported it slipping into private gardens, skirting close to people, and most troubling to officials, showing little inclination to run away.

Its behavior strongly suggested that it had been fed, teaching it to associate humans with food and reward, said Peter Sunde, a Danish wolf expert and professor at Aarhus University.

“If they begin to regard humans as a food source, then that’s the road to trouble,” he said, explaining that authorities take an uncompromising stance toward wolves that approach people.

“A fed wolf is a dead wolf,” he said.

The authorities designated it a “problem wolf” and effectively put out a warrant. For about a week, armed wildlife officers patrolled the area, while thermal drones hunted for the animal’s heat signature after dark. Residents were asked to report sightings.

Wolf experts said it wasn’t really possible to tranquilize it for transport to another area because Denmark has little open land and the wolf would likely behave the same wherever it was and pose the same threat.

Then, on Thursday evening, came the showdown. Wildlife officers found two wolves in a woodsy area near the town where it had been spotted. When the animals emerged, an officer was waiting nearby with a rifle.

One wolf bolted. The other, the “problem,” did not.

As the remaining wolf tried to move around him, the officer fired from about 10 meters away, striking it in the right side and killing it.

The political debate about the wolves has been intensifying since the animals returned to Denmark. As their numbers have grown, so has the divide between those who see the wolf as an important part of the country’s wildlife and those who question whether there is room for it at all in a small, densely populated country. Denmark has few other major predators — there are no bears here.

Mr. Rabjerg Madsen said he wants more flexible rules for killing problem wolves; some lawmakers have gone further, calling for dramatically fewer wolves — or none at all.

“It’s obviously not a happy occasion to have to shoot a wolf, but it was necessary,” he said at the news conference on Friday.

Animal-welfare groups have pushed back, arguing that wolves play an important role in Denmark’s ecosystem by keeping the population of deer in check.

“The mere sight of a wolf can make people afraid,” said Thomas Søby of Dyrenes Beskyttelse, the Danish animal-welfare organization.

But, he added, “We have to learn to live with it.”

item.title: As Army Fails to Protect Palestinians, Israeli Leaders Sympathize With Settlers
item.description:
The Israeli army’s faltering attempts this week to rescue two Palestinian families who have been besieged in their West Bank homes by violent Jewish settlers prompted a striking statement on Friday morning from Israel’s defense minister, Israel Katz.

He said he wanted to get the Israeli military out of the business of protecting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank from rampaging settlers and would try to shift the responsibility to the Israeli police.

As a practical matter, only the Israel Defense Forces have the thousands of personnel needed to patrol and respond quickly to attacks in the scores of communities plagued by settler violence this year. Moreover, experts say that giving responsibility to the Israeli police would essentially put the fox in charge of the henhouse, because the police are overseen by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, an extremist settler himself.

For Mr. Katz, an ambitious member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party who hopes to succeed him as its leader, his recommendation was a political move to duck responsibility, analysts said.

Rather, for example, than letting the army use administrative detention to lock up settlers who break the law, a crucial tool previously used by the government, Mr. Katz is saying he prefers that soldiers avoid getting between settlers and Palestinians in their moments of “friction,” as some Israelis euphemistically call such attacks.

“It is not the I.D.F.’s role, and it is unable, to address the enforcement of civil matters” in the West Bank in light of the “welcome increase” in the number of Israeli settlers there, Mr. Katz said.

As the occupying power, the Israeli military alone bears responsibility under international law for protecting Palestinian civilians in the West Bank and has held authority for law and order since Israel captured the territory in the 1967 war.

The police have a division in the West Bank, given the hundreds of thousands of Israeli civilians living there in settlements widely considered illegal under international law. But handing the police responsibility for protecting Palestinian civilians could be seen as another step toward creeping annexation of the territory, a goal shared by many in Mr. Netanyahu’s government.

On Friday, settlers who have trapped two Palestinian families in their homes in the village of Qusra all week set up a tent there, before soldiers took it down, according to the local mayor, Abdul Azim al-Wadi, and an Israeli military statement. Settlers, however, remained in the vicinity as of early evening, while soldiers stood nearby, Mr. al-Wadi said.

“If the Israeli authorities want stability, they need to arrest the settlers,” he said. “That’s the only solution.”

In its statement, the military said that throughout the day, “soldiers operating in the area remained engaged in efforts to evacuate the Israeli civilians from the area of the closed military zone.”

For years, Israeli leaders including Mr. Netanyahu have downplayed settler violence as the work of a “handful of kids,” or of a few dozen or a few hundred wayward youth, often saying that many came from broken homes, suggesting they should be pitied rather than prosecuted. The effort to minimize the violence has continued even as the number of Palestinians killed by settlers has climbed since January, paired with beatings and the torching of hundreds of houses, car and mosques.

But now, with an army that has defeated vastly more powerful enemies failing to achieve the task of making it possible for two Palestinian families to live safely in their own homes, members of Mr. Netanyahu’s government are making clear on which side of the issue they stand.

Not surprisingly, Mr. Ben-Gvir, the minister overseeing the police, insisted that the settlers’ siege in Qusra was the military’s responsibility.

In a radio interview Thursday, he said he wasn’t familiar with the details of the Qusra situation but hastened to take the side of settlers encroaching on Palestinian communities. “There are some among them who truly need to be arrested and addressed; I’m not saying all of them are righteous,” he allowed. “But most of these guys, who settle the land of Israel, who build outposts — I admire them.”

Mr. Ben-Gvir, who leads the supremacist Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, party, also argued that the real violence was not being committed by settlers. “I know what’s happening here in Judea and Samaria,” he said, using the biblical names for the West Bank. “I live here. For now, the danger is that the Arabs throw stones, the Arabs throw Molotov cocktails, the Arabs shoot.”

Mr. Netanyahu himself has not addressed the standoff in Qusra. But a lawmaker from his party, Amit Halevi, chose Thursday to meet and be photographed with a group of extremist settlers, including one who has been sanctioned by several countries for violence. Mr. Halevi did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The events in Qusra are forcing the issue of settler violence — or, as a growing number of prominent Israelis now call it, “Jewish terrorism” — to center stage in the midst of an enormously consequential political campaign ahead of Israeli elections in October.

Members of the political opposition lambasted the government for failing to curb the violence. Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who once led the umbrella organization for West Bank settlements, called it “acts of terrorism.” He faulted the Netanyahu government for responding so slowly that, according to the U.S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, the Trump administration had urged it to intervene in Qusra.

“We need to denounce this and root out violence from within, not wait for the Americans to tell us to do so,” Mr. Bennett said in a radio interview.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff who now is the front-runner in opinion polls for prime minister, called the Qusra situation a “severe expression of the failures and weakness” of the government.

“In the face of anarchy and violent violations of the law by an extremist minority, the government is abandoning I.D.F. commanders to fight the battle alone,” he wrote on social media.

Israeli military officials have long complained that the police take a lax approach to violent settlers and that judges rarely impose tough sentences. But critics of the military say it, too, often hesitates in the face of settler violence and fails to use all the tools at its disposal.

On Wednesday, a group of army reservists released an open letter calling on the military “to act with determination against Jewish terrorism” and “to uproot it.” The letter, addressed to Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the army’s chief of staff, had 465 signatures by Friday, organizers said.

“Nationalistic terror in Judea and Samaria is not stopping,” the letter reads. “We are required again and again to stand between ‘friction incidents’ in territory under our responsibility, without a real mandate to prevent them.”

The letter adds: “The lack of backing and guidance from the I.D.F.’s senior leadership, the turning of a blind eye to Jewish terrorism and to the known places from which it emanates, and at times even the political echelon’s support for it, endanger us and leave us abandoned.”

Moshe Karadi, who commanded the Israeli police from 2004 to 2007, recalled the police taking aggressive action against settlers in the past but said that it was unclear that certain police commanders could be counted upon now, because of Mr. Ben-Gvir’s influence over them.

Mr. Karadi called the handling of the settlers’ siege this week in Qusra a “disgrace,” saying that “terrorists need to be handled with force.”

Still, he said the military made a strategic error by not calling the police to remove the settlers immediately after they started besieging the Palestinians. Soldiers are trained to fight Palestinians, not Israelis, he said, while the police are trained to confront both.

“In my opinion, it appears the officers in the military are afraid of the political level,” he said. “They don’t know how their actions will be interpreted so they prefer to do nothing.”

item.title: France’s Top Court Strikes Down Ban on Social Media for Children
item.description:
France’s highest court on Friday rejected the government’s move to ban people under 15 from using social media, a stinging setback to President Emmanuel Macron, who has made the measure a centerpiece of his legislative agenda in his final year in office.

The Constitutional Council, France’s closest equivalent to the Supreme Court, said that, although such a ban could be justified, its current provisions constituted a “disproportionate infringement on freedom of expression and communication,” according to a statement released on Friday.

The council said the ban, which lawmakers passed in July, was too wide-ranging — it could apply to platforms that did not necessarily pose risks to children’s health and safety — and that it did not take into account the age, maturity or family situation of children. The council also found that the ban would infringe on privacy, because it would require everyone to prove their age on social media platforms.

France was the first European country to pass a law restricting young people’s access to social media, following in the footsteps of Australia, which passed a similar law in December. Denmark and Spain are preparing similar legislation, but the court’s decision underscores the legal and practical hurdles to these efforts. Critics say they are ineffective and can have unintended consequences.

Left-wing lawmakers, who had opposed the law and petitioned the council to weigh in on its legality, praised the decision. Arthur Delaporte, a socialist lawmaker in the National Assembly, said in a statement that the Council’s verdict had proven their arguments valid and that the law had been “drafted in haste,” and was “too vague, too broad.”

Mr. Macron still hopes to enact a law before he leaves office next spring. His office said in a statement that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu would develop a “legally sound” version of the law that would also align with new European Union-wide regulations that are being drafted in Brussels.

The statement added that Mr. Macron remained committed to protecting “the best interests and health of our children.”

But legal experts said European countries were limited in their ability to go after foreign technology companies because of jurisdictional issues. And the European Union already does much of what France could legally do through the bloc’s Digital Services Act, a law enacted in 2022 that seeks to protect children from harmful effects of social media, among other goals.

“The protection of minors with regard to social networks is no longer really a national issue on which the government and candidates can commit,” Benjamin Morel, a constitutional scholar at Panthéon-Assas University in Paris, said on social media.

item.title: American Missionary Kidnapped in Niger Soon to Be Reunited With Family
item.description:
A mission organization said on Friday that a pilot who was kidnapped while working for the group in the West African country of Niger last year was in “good health” after his release.

The missionary pilot, Kevin Rideout, was seized from his home in Niamey, the capital of Niger, in October. The organization, called Serving in Mission, said in a statement that Mr. Rideout was with U.S. officials as he waited to be reunited with his loved ones.

“We are grateful to confirm that our good friend and brother in Christ, Kevin Rideout, has been released,” the statement read. The mission added that he was in “good health in the care of U.S. officials” and would soon be reunited with his wife, Krista; their four children; and his extended family.

“Krista and the rest of Kevin’s family are profoundly grateful for the prayers offered on their behalf by people around the world throughout his captivity,” the statement added.

Mr. Rideout’s release was earlier reported by The New York Times based on the account of two U.S. officials, who spoke on Thursday on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. How and where he was released were not yet clear, the officials said at the time, and it was also unclear which group had held him at the end of his captivity. Mr. Rideout’s release had been a major priority for the White House and for the military’s Africa Command.

In May, the French journalist and researcher Wassim Nasr, who has been monitoring jihadist groups in the area for several years, said that Mr. Rideout was being held in Ménaka, a region in Mali just over the border with Niger. That area is mostly controlled by a local branch of the Islamic State.

For years, Mali and Niger have been battling insurgents affiliated with Al Qaeda and the Islamic State. In April, Al Qaeda-linked militants launched coordinated attacks across Mali, seizing a major city and killing the country’s defense minister.

item.title: With Trump’s Hamas Deal in Peril, Kushner Set to Visit Israel for Gaza Talks
item.description:
Jared Kushner, President Trump’s senior aide and son-in-law, is set to visit Israel early next week, according to four people familiar with the plans, days after the Israeli government rejected a U.S.-brokered disarmament deal with Hamas.

Mr. Kushner is expected to meet with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss Gaza, the people said, speaking on condition of anonymity to divulge details about Mr. Kushner’s schedule.

The deal, agreed to earlier this month between Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace and the militant group Hamas, called for the disarmament of Palestinian factions in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces there.

The Board of Peace is a new international organization chaired by Mr. Trump that has focused on plans for governing and rebuilding Gaza. Mr. Kushner is a senior member of its executive board and was involved in cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israel.

Mr. Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel rejected the deal, a move that was seen as an appeal to his right-wing voting base ahead of national elections in October. Yet the prime minister also ordered the Israeli military to pause its strikes in Gaza, in an apparent effort to appease the Trump administration.

For days after the announcement, the Israeli military conducted no airstrikes in Gaza, until Wednesday, when the military carried out a fresh attack, saying it was targeting Hamas militants. It conducted further attacks on Thursday.

Hamas officials have condemned the strikes, calling on mediating countries in the region to pressure Israel to halt them.

Hamas remains in control of about half of Gaza, where most of its people live. The group said that among those killed by Israel this week was the head of the police force in the Gaza City area.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza and former United Nations envoy, will join Mr. Kushner in Israel, according to two of the people with knowledge of the visit. Mr. Mladenov has played a leading role in the negotiations with Hamas over disarmament, frequently meeting with officials from the group in Egypt.

Mr. Kushner and Mr. Mladenov were also expected to visit Egypt next week to meet with regional mediators, according to two of the people.

The deal with Hamas says that, as part of the disarmament process, Israel should first uphold its side of the cease-fire, which was agreed to in October last year. That includes halting airstrikes and allowing more aid into Gaza.

The 15-point document leaves elements of the disarmament process vague, however. It calls for a “gradual, sequential and timebound manner” for decommissioning and storing heavy weapons, with an exact timetable still to be determined.

It adds that, at the “end of the process,” the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, will “hold, control or store weapons in Gaza.” The committee, a body of Palestinian technocrats, was assembled by the Board of Peace to take over governing Gaza under the board’s supervision.

Many Israelis remain skeptical that Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace can successfully disarm Hamas. The group has long touted armed struggle against Israel as the core of its ideology, and members have said they regard disarmament as tantamount to surrender.

item.title: A Prominent Mexican Politician Says U.S. Revoked His Visa
item.description:
One of the most prominent figures in Mexican politics, a former president’s son, says that the United States has revoked his visa, inflaming tensions between the Trump administration and Mexico’s governing party.

On Thursday night, the politician, Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, released an angry, three-page letter to President Trump asking him if he knew about the decision to revoke his visa. He called the move “a crude and perverse dirty trick,” carried out by officials who target people like him for refusing to “submit to their authoritarian, divisive ambitions.”

The White House and the U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The State Department has increasingly revoked visas of officials in Latin America, including some whom U.S. officials have later accused of corruption. Mr. López Beltrán has been accused of corruption by his political opponents, but he has denied the allegations and the authorities have never made formal accusations against him.

In his letter, Mr. López Beltrán said that there were no grounds to revoke his visa because he was honest. But he added that he didn’t mind, because he had no desire to visit the United States “during these decadent and lamentable times of hatred, racism, drug addiction, family breakdown, social discontent and sorrow.” He called Mr. Trump “arrogant” if he was aware of the decision to revoke his visa, and called on him to fire Secretary of State Marco Rubio if he was not.

The developments put President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico in a bind.

Mr. López Beltrán is the son of former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who is Ms. Sheinbaum’s political mentor and still a key leader of Morena, Mexico’s dominant political party. Mr. López Beltrán was a top party official until May, when he stepped down to run for Mexico’s Congress.

On Friday, Ms. Sheinbaum called such visa cancellations politically motivated.

“They are not applied consistently across all countries, as they would be if the intent were truly related to crime,” she said in her daily news conference. “This is clearly an act of interference in Mexican politics; I see no other reason.” When asked about Mr. López Beltrán’s letter, she said he has a right to speak out.

Ms. Sheinbaum has attempted to walk a political tightrope amid an intensifying pressure campaign from Washington. The Trump administration has called on her government to do more against cartels and corrupt politicians, while many officials in her party have called on her to stand up to Mr. Trump. She has forged a positive personal relationship with Mr. Trump, while publicly criticizing his administration and quietly increasing cooperation with the U.S. government on security.

The State Department said on Monday that under the Trump administration it had revoked more than 175,000 visas granted to foreign citizens. It said it had rescinded most over criminal accusations, including for drugs, assault and fraud.

Yet many visa cancellations have also had a political backdrop. The State Department has said it had revoked visas of people who participated in pro-Palestinian protests or who celebrated the assassination of the right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, for instance.

The U.S. government has also revoked visas to target foreign leaders, ambassadors and other officials, as well as judges and journalists — while reinstating visas for some like-minded allies. The State Department has explicitly said it was using the threat of canceling visas as part of its strategy to exert more control over Latin America.

The State Department has canceled the visas of Mexican governors, federal and state legislators, and mayors in states along the northern border.

Because of the confidentiality of visa records, the State Department rarely discusses details. But of the known cases in Mexico, a majority of those with visa restrictions are members of Morena. Several of those affected have said publicly that their visa restrictions stem from administrative issues, not direct accusations against them.

In the past, the U.S. government had pulled the visas of former Mexican governors, but only after they had left office. Those measures usually followed — or preceded — sanctions for cartel corruption or federal indictments for racketeering and money laundering.

Chantal Flores contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Britain’s Farage Takes a Page From Trump’s Playbook Amid Investigations
item.description:
Nigel Farage, Britain’s leading right-wing politician, faced a dilemma last month.

What do you do when the inquiries and accusations are piling up? The police are looking into one of your donors. You are being investigated for potentially breaking Parliament’s rules because you didn’t report a £5 million gift. The news media are publishing new allegations almost daily.

For Mr. Farage, the leader of the Reform U.K. party, the answer appears to have been clear: Attack your critics, undermine the regulatory or judicial processes by labeling them illegitimate before they conclude, and seek pre-emptive absolution from “the people” — your most loyal supporters.

He was borrowing a page from a playbook honed over the years by other embattled populists like President Trump, Marine Le Pen, the French far-right leader, and Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister. Mr. Farage resigned his parliamentary seat and immediately ran for it again in the resulting special election.

On Friday, he declared himself completely vindicated by his victory in the contest in Clacton, in eastern England.

“I wanted the people of Clacton, the voters of this constituency, to be my judge,” he said in an early-morning victory speech while votes were still being counted. “Not the mainstream media in Britain and the political establishment who paint us out to be criminals and bad people every day. I asked the voters of Clacton to be my jury, and the verdict has now come in.”

The result was hardly surprising. Mr. Farage won in a safe Reform U.K. seat, collecting 63 percent of the vote in an election that all the other major parties boycotted and called a stunt. His main challenger? A novelty candidate called Count Binface, who wears a trash can over his head.

The question now is whether the gambit will work, or whether British voters outside of his party’s core base will continue to pay attention to the questions swirling around Mr. Farage about donations and expensive gifts. In the weeks since revelations about his undisclosed benefits were first published in The Guardian and The Sunday Times, his personal poll ratings have fallen, and Reform’s position in national polls has slipped.

Within hours of his speech on Friday, the office of the parliamentary standards commissioner restarted its investigation into Mr. Farage’s failure to declare the 5 million pound gift (about $6.7 million) from a British crypto-billionaire based in Thailand. (Mr. Farage has said he didn’t need to register it because it was a personal gift given before he was a member of Parliament.)

Yet Mr. Farage has proved to be a resilient political survivor who successfully tapped into public anger about successive British governments. His decades-long campaign to limit immigration remains one of the most potent issues in the country, and Reform is still polling within the margin of error of the governing Labour Party and above the Conservatives.

And he is not wrong to notice that the go-on-the-offense political strategy has worked well for several of his peers across the world who, like him, have denied any wrongdoing.

Take Mr. Trump. After leaving office in 2021, he faced a battery of criminal charges and civil lawsuits for accusations including falsifying business records, illegally retaining documents containing national security secrets, trying to reverse the results of the 2020 election, and sexual abuse and defamation.

Mr. Trump railed about the “witch hunts” being conducted by the “establishment” and accused the news media of being the “enemy of the people.” He said judges, prosecutors, F.B.I. agents, intelligence officers and election officials were all corrupt or incompetent — or both.

But most of all, he insisted that none of it would matter to the American voters.

“Your victory will be our ultimate vindication, your liberty will be our ultimate reward and the unprecedented success of the United States of America will be my ultimate and absolute revenge,” Mr. Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024.

By November 2024, when more than 77 million people chose to return Mr. Trump to office, most of the criminal and civil charges against him had either stalled, been dismissed or been nullified by the Supreme Court.

Tony Travers, a professor of politics at the London School of Economics, said Mr. Farage and his allies are betting that he can convince the British public to see the Reform leader in the same way that many Americans see the president — as a victim of unfair persecution.

“That is pretty similar to Donald Trump, it seems to me,” Mr. Travers said. “That people are prepared to overlook all the cryptocurrency stuff and the self-enrichment that’s going on, because somehow he’s different, he’s an outsider.”

In France, Ms. Le Pen was found guilty last year of embezzlement by a criminal court and barred from running for public office for five years. She called the ruling a “political” attempt to thwart her.

“I’m not going to submit to a democratic denial so easily,” Ms. Le Pen added.

When the five-year ban on running for office was lifted by an appeals court last month, she immediately declared: “This evening, I am a candidate in the presidential election.” Like Mr. Trump, she is betting that voters in a national election will look past her legal troubles.

On Friday, Jordan Bardella, a protégé of Ms. Le Pen and the president of their National Rally Party, congratulated Mr. Farage on his victory, writing on social media: “Nigel Farage had the courage and dignity to submit himself once again to the judgment of the voters, the sole masters in a democracy.”

Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, has used similar political tactics to try to undermine bribery and corruption charges that were leveled against him years ago.

He was indicted in 2019 on charges of giving or offering lucrative favors to several media tycoons in exchange for favorable news coverage or gifts worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. He appropriated one of Mr. Trump’s favorite phrases, calling the corruption investigations a “witch hunt,” as well as “a joke” and “an absurdity.”

But in 2022 he was re-elected as prime minister in what he characterized as a total rejection of the charges against him.

“We have won a huge vote of confidence from the people of Israel,” he said.

It remains to be seen whether Mr. Farage’s attempt to appeal to “the people” over the outcome of the investigations will succeed in Britain.

His by-election victory on Thursday was in a tiny, Reform-friendly corner of the country, hardly a nationwide referendum on his actions. And, as a general election does not have to be held until 2029, it may be some time before we find out.

]]>

item.title: Jason Arday, Cambridge Scholar Who Resigned Under Scrutiny, Is Found Dead
item.description:
Jason Arday, the former Cambridge University scholar whose remarkable rise to stardom was followed by a rapid fall from grace in recent weeks, has died, his family said on Friday.

“Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse” in the years since he accepted a role at Cambridge, his family wrote in a statement. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”

The Metropolitan Police of London said that an ambulance was called on Friday afternoon to a South London residence connected to Mr. Arday after a report that a man there had been found unresponsive. The man was pronounced dead at the scene, the police said, without confirming his identity, in keeping with British police practice.

The death was being “treated as unexpected” but was not believed to be suspicious, the police said.

“We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news,” Professor Deborah Prentice, the Cambridge vice-chancellor, said in a statement. “Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”

Mr. Arday, who was 41, grew up in a working-class quarter of South London, the child of Ghanaian immigrants. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties. He wrote in his memoir that he could not speak until age 11 and could not read until age 18, charting a remarkable trajectory from nonverbal preteen to Ph.D.

Mr. Arday, who had written and lectured on racism in higher education, became Cambridge’s youngest Black professor in 2023 when the university hired him for a prestigious post, an established chair of education at the school’s Jesus College.

Last month, a public firestorm over Mr. Arday’s career erupted after a blog post accused him of plagiarism in his dissertation and embellishing his personal story. It was written by a scholar known for work suggesting that Black people were genetically predisposed to be less intelligent than white people.

Scrutiny intensified ahead of the publication of Mr. Arday’s memoir on Tuesday by Simon & Schuster, as journalists found more inconsistencies in his story. He resigned from Cambridge last week.

Allegations about Mr. Arday’s work circulated within Cambridge for years, but the institution disregarded repeated warnings about possible duplication in Mr. Arday’s work, according to the academic integrity site Retraction Watch.

The elite university initially defended Mr. Arday but in a letter sent to faculty on Tuesday promised an independent investigation of his hiring and called the case “an aberration” and “troubling.”

Some faculty had supported Mr. Arday. Others signed an open letter questioning the university’s handling of the allegations and criticizing it for “crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential.”

Nick Clark, who has known Mr. Arday since childhood, described him in an interview last week as a caring person who would go out of his way to make others feel comfortable in everyday social settings. Mr. Arday was modest when discussing his career with his friends, said Mr. Clark, but those who knew him personally took pride in his accomplishments. “He’s always been that kind, caring, friendly character,” he added. “That’s Jason.”

“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son,” Mr. Arday’s family said in its statement.

The intense attention took a toll on Mr. Arday, he wrote in a blog post upon resigning from Cambridge. “The years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack,” he wrote, adding, “The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.”

Neil Vigdor and Leo Sands contributed reporting.

item.title: The Taliban Kicked the U.S. Out of Afghanistan. Now They Want It Back.
item.description:
Five years after driving the United States out of Afghanistan, the Taliban are inviting it to come back — with diplomats and cash, but no military.

“We consider the chapter of war to have come to an end, and from now on, we want relations based on mutual respect and a new chapter of positive engagement,” Afghanistan’s foreign minister, Amir Khan Muttaqi, said in an interview with The New York Times in Kabul.

Mr. Muttaqi said the United States could “reopen its embassy, maintain a diplomatic presence and invest” in Afghanistan’s vast mineral wealth, dams and roads — projects that three U.S. administrations and their allies spent billions trying to develop, and that the Taliban insurgency spent two decades trying to dismantle.

The public overture, the first by such a high-ranking Taliban official in years, is the Afghan government’s latest push in a long effort to extract the country from isolation, with mixed results.

Over the past year, the Taliban administration has signed a defense partnership with Russia and secured dozens of trade agreements with Central Asian neighbors like Uzbekistan. Some of its officials regularly travel to Gulf countries and have met with Syria’s president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. It is also cooperating with European countries eager to deport Afghan migrants.

The government would see renewed engagement with the Trump administration, with its appetite for commercial diplomacy and little consideration for human rights, as the crowning achievement of its diplomatic efforts, according to five former U.S. and Afghan officials familiar with Kabul’s approach.

The Taliban argue that they have brought order and security across Afghanistan, cleaned its administration of corruption and created favorable conditions for foreign investment.

But efforts to engage with the United States have stalled.

“There is no appetite in D.C.,” said Hassan Abbas, a U.S.-based scholar and the author of a recent book on the Taliban in power. “No one wants to touch this topic. Everyone wants to forget about Afghanistan.”

In fact, the Trump administration has further distanced itself from the Taliban over the past year.

It has moved closer to one of Afghanistan’s neighbors, Pakistan, which launched dozens of airstrikes on Afghanistan earlier this year. It is embroiled in a conflict with another neighbor, Iran, one of the Taliban’s few steady partners. It has ​also designated the Taliban as a state sponsor of wrongful detention, paused issuing visas for Afghans and barred them from traveling to the United States.

The Taliban have also rebuffed President Trump on the few things he has publicly asked for, including regaining control of Bagram Air Base, which U.S. forces occupied for 20 years; the return of U.S. weapons abandoned in Afghanistan; and the release of a U.S. prisoner whom the Taliban deny holding.

“No Afghan wants or can tolerate the military presence of another country on Afghan soil, as history has demonstrated,” Mr. Muttaqi said at the foreign ministry this week, sitting in a plush armchair with the white flag of the Taliban behind him.

In a written response to questions, the U.S. State Department rejected the prospect of normalization. The response, attributed to “a department spokesperson,” said the Taliban had failed to make Afghanistan more stable and uphold counterterrorism commitments, instead allowing terrorist groups to use Afghanistan as a launchpad for attacks.

It said the United States engages with the Taliban “only when it is in the interest of the American people.”

A veteran member of the Taliban and a central figure in past negotiations between the United States and the group before it swept back to power, Mr. Muttaqi said his administration wanted to reopen diplomatic missions in the United States.

Mr. Muttaqi, 55, also confirmed that Afghanistan was negotiating migration agreements with European countries.

“We have made progress in this area, and we hope to make significant further progress in the future,” Mr. Muttaqi said, without elaborating.

In recent months, the Afghan government held several bilateral meetings on migration with countries like Germany and France. A delegation of five Afghan diplomats also met more than 20 diplomats from 15 E.U. countries in Brussels in June to discuss repatriating rejected asylum seekers and convicted criminals, according to three participants and an official briefed on the discussions.

One of the participants, an Afghan diplomat, said that in Europe, the taboo of talking to the Taliban had been broken and that Afghanistan would now engage in bilateral discussions with all interested countries to finalize agreements.

Still, no European country recognizes the Taliban administration as Afghanistan’s legitimate authority, and the government remains a pariah excluded from international bodies like the United Nations and the International Monetary Fund.

The Taliban’s ultraconservative leader, Sheikh Haibatullah Akhundzada, faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity over the persecution of Afghan women and girls. And the United States has frozen billions of dollars from the Afghan Central Bank.

And yet, a growing chorus of analysts and former diplomats in the United States is calling for renewed U.S.-Afghan dialogue beyond counterterrorism cooperation against the Islamic State and prisoner negotiations.

Mr. Trump has the opportunity to do what President Joseph R. Biden Jr. could not, said Robin Raphel, a former U.S. diplomat with extensive experience in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Moving past the current paralysis, Ms. Raphel said, could create new access to minerals, strengthen relations with Afghanistan’s Central Asian neighbors, and counter China and Russia, which do trade and have diplomats in the country.

“But that requires hands-on engagement through a U.S. presence in Kabul, which remains a hard sell in Washington,” Ms. Raphel said.

In an initial exchange with The Times earlier this year, Mr. Muttaqi highlighted Afghanistan’s mines as a potential starting point for a “new chapter for the two countries.”

“I view President Trump’s deal-making ability, pragmatic approach and decisiveness as factors that can facilitate constructive engagement with his administration,” Mr. Muttaqi said.

Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow for South Asia at the D.C.-based Atlantic Council, said minerals were the right pitch to make to the Trump administration. Afghanistan holds vast untapped reserves of lithium, copper and iron ore, as well as rare earth elements that are on the U.S. Geological Survey’s list of critical minerals.

“Values-based considerations like brutality and the Taliban’s horrific treatment of women and girls would not necessarily keep this administration from engaging with the Taliban, particularly if that could help advance U.S. economic interests,” Mr. Kugelman said.

Discussions around Afghanistan’s mineral wealth are not new.

The United States spent nearly $1 billion between 2004 and 2021 to develop Afghanistan’s extractive industry but failed to accomplish any “tangible progress,” according to a 2023 report from SIGAR, the defunct U.S. government oversight agency for Afghanistan. The Taliban administration now holds mining investment deals with companies from China, Iran and Qatar, among others.

Beyond the United States, Mr. Muttaqi called on any country to invest in Afghanistan, where the Taliban administration is in desperate need of foreign capital.

Half of its estimated 45 million people require humanitarian assistance dwindled by U.S. aid cuts last year, according to the United Nations. About four million Afghans have returned from neighboring Pakistan and Iran since early 2025, in one of the largest episodes of reverse migration in decades.

Pakistan, which used to be Afghanistan’s primary trade partner, has closed its border over security concerns, sending the Taliban scrambling for alternative avenues of trade with Central Asian states, Iran and India.

During the interview, Mr. Muttaqi brushed aside a question about whether his government’s crackdown on women and girls was a barrier to international recognition. Earlier this year, he declared the government’s move to keep them out of secondary education was “temporary” — an argument the Taliban also used during their first rule, between 1996 and 2001, when Mr. Muttaqi served as education minister, and immediately after their return to power in 2021.

Mr. Abbas, the academic, said he expected the Taliban to remain isolated as long as they refused to move on their most extreme policies — which are largely dictated out of the city of Kandahar, the group’s spiritual heartland and home to Sheikh Akhundzada.

“Without compromising, without changing anything that they stand for, it is a no-starter,” Mr. Abbas said. “Something has to happen, and the Taliban are not offering that.”

Yaqoob Akbary and Safiullah Padshah contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Heat is Hammering Europe, Again. Here’s What That Looks Like.
item.description:
For the fifth time this summer, Europe is sweating under an intense heat wave.

The signs of a persistently hot and exceptionally dry summer are everywhere. Brown, dusty patches have replaced verdant lawns in London’s parks. Major rivers like the Danube and the Rhine have retreated, exposing sandbars. The conditions have created a tinderbox for wildfires. Forests in Germany and in Bosnia and Herzegovina were ablaze on Friday, while firefighters were battling to save thousands of acres and hundreds of homes in Britain, France, Greece and Spain.

Weeks of relentless heat have tested the continent’s resolve, buckling train lines, shorting power grids and smashing records that had been set only recently. The combination of a “heat dome” phenomenon and the effects of climate change have left Europe wondering whether suffocating summers are the new norm.

Siviri, Greece

Working to extinguish a wildfire on Thursday. Hundreds of tourists were evacuated from beaches in the area as flames bore down on two resorts.

Locarno, Switzerland

Walking along a sandbar formed by low water levels in the Maggia River delta on Thursday.

Nijmegen, Netherlands

Boats stranded by lower water levels on Friday.

Rome

Cooling off with an industrial fan on Tuesday. Living outside in extreme heat is a particular challenge.

Mount Cincar, Bosnia and Herzegovina

Wild horses drinking at a reservoir on Thursday. Hundreds roam a plateau at the foot of the mountain, relying on such artificial sources for water during droughts.

Lokva Rogoznica, Croatia

Emergency services battling a large wildfire on Thursday night.

London

Parched parklands on Primrose Hill on Wednesday. Britain is on track for the warmest summer on record for average temperature, breaking a record set last year.

item.title: Inside Russia’s Giant Push to Upend a Tiny Country
item.description:
It resembled in many ways a summer camp. Barbecues and beach volleyball games were on offer. A wellness spa was called “Relax and Have Fun.”

The men and women who attended the program at a resort complex in a remote part of Serbia also took part in more sinister activities, like learning to break through police cordons and set buildings on fire. They donned flak jackets and trained with assault rifles.

Their counselors, it turned out, were operatives with ties to Russia’s military intelligence service, known as the GRU. Their purpose, according to intelligence officials from three countries who described the activities, was to build a cadre of disciplined shock troops trained in election interference.

The target was tiny Moldova, a country of about three million people that carries outsize importance for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The Kremlin’s campaign included methods familiar elsewhere in the West, like hacking and disinformation. But in Moldova, its intervention went further than perhaps anywhere else outside Ukraine, and stands as one of the most extensive and audacious plots to date in Mr. Putin’s effort to destabilize the West, the three Western intelligence officials say.

Besides the camp in Serbia, Russian agents ran training programs in Bosnia and Moscow that were designed to turn pro-Russian Moldovans into foot soldiers. Moscow paid hundreds of Orthodox Moldovan priests to recruit voters and to push Russian narratives from the pulpit. And it spent hundreds of millions of dollars on a sophisticated vote-buying scheme financed by a Moldovan billionaire in exile and conceived and operated from Skolkovo, the Kremlin’s knockoff Silicon Valley outside Moscow.

Moscow’s campaign has not stopped. This spring, Russian missiles targeted energy infrastructure that provided service to Moldova, polluting waterways and disrupting electricity flows.

This article is based on interviews with activists who took part in the Russian effort; senior Moldovan law enforcement and security officials; and more than half a dozen European and American intelligence officials. The New York Times also reviewed thousands of documents related to Russia’s attempts to interfere in Moldova’s elections.

Many of those interviewed insisted on speaking anonymously, either to discuss sensitive security operations or because they feared retribution.

Details about Russian efforts in Moldova have emerged in court cases and local reporting, but the scope and extent of the campaign, including the vote-buying scheme and role of Russia’s intelligence services, has not been previously reported.

Publicly, Russian officials have denied interfering in Moldova’s affairs, and have dismissed accusations that Moscow is trying to undermine the West. Last December, Mr. Putin, in an address to military commanders, castigated European leaders for “stoking hysteria” over the threat from Russia.

Soon afterward, though, he gathered the leaders for a secret briefing to deliver the exact opposite message, according to officials from two countries with knowledge of the episode. Their goal for 2026, Mr. Putin told them, is “the collapse of NATO and the E.U. from within,” the people said.
